newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain breathes life into private finance scheme.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain breathes life into private finance scheme.

text.p: Britain's Private Finance Initiative (PFI) could be seen as the natural culmination of Conservative prime minister Margaret Thatcher's mission to make Britain a free market economy and curb the public sector.

So it is perhaps ironic that it is a Labour government which is now trying to salvage the floundering scheme to get private investors to finance costly public ventures such as the building of roads and hospitals.

Five years after its launch the PFI has garnered only a fraction of the business its Conservative creators envisaged and has earned itself the alternative tags Pretty Farcical Idea and Plethora of Failed Investments.
The scheme had become mired in bureaucracy, prohibitive costs and the historic suspicion between Britain's private and public sectors.
The new Labour government under reformist leader Tony Blair made tackling PFI's problems one of its priorities within days of winning the May 1 election.

Given Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon's Brown's pledge to keep tight limits on public spending, the PFI is central to the government's pledges to improve health, education and transport.
Geoffrey Robinson, a former chief executive of Jaguar Cars and the hugely successful engineering group Transtec, was appointed Paymaster General with a remit to make the PFI work.

Another financial wizard, Malcolm Bates of Pearl Insurance, was appointed to report on the scheme's failings. He has already submitted his findings to the government and they will be published on June 23.
GOVERNMENT TARGETS
The government has pledged to reform the scheme and says it wants at least 10 billion pounds ($16 billion) of PFI projects underway in the next three years.

It is not a huge target until set beside the seven billion pounds of projects that have been signed or carried out since the PFI was launched in 1992 by the Conservatives who were ousted in the May election after 18 years in power.

Half of that figure includes the contract for a new rail link from the Channel Tunnel into London, described by one newspaper as having "financial doom written all over it." Almost all the remainder were projects valued at less than 10 million pounds.

Many of the failings that Bates is likely to identify have already been aired by the media, the Confederation of British Industry (CBI) and companies that have been involved in tendering for PFI projects.
The CBI wants to see a drastic reduction in the bureacracy surrounding the PFI, but it also believes a change in political will is needed.

"If the private sector is to take the downside risk, it also needs to to know that it can take the upside, and take it without being publicly pilloried for making high profits," CBI director Adair Turner told a recent conference.

This could be an area of discomfort for Blair's government which is planning a hefty "windfall tax" on privatised utilities that have heaped up huge profits since being privatised under the Conservatives.
Businesses themselves are also wary of any change in political climate that could leave them lambasted as "fat cats" as the bosses of the private utilities have been.
"The public can be easily offended by charges imposed by private operators, even when signed and sealed with the government of the day," wrote one newspaper columnist.
"Add in a public political scrap, with 'fat cat' accusations against the contractor, or even against the financing banks, and many companies may decide the aggravation is not worth the candle."

The government has already removed one costly and much derided element of the PFI, which required all government capital projects to be evaluated for private finance -- even if they were clearly unsuitable.
According to the CBI, this "universal testing" requirement created masses of unwanted procedure and huge costs for companies bidding for projects which would never come to fruition.
The National Health Service invited tenders for the construction of 24 hospitals, even though only a handful of these were ever expected to be built.
Companies tendering for the work would have no idea which contract was likely to go ahead.

The CBI estimates it cost a company around two million pounds to get to the final stages of tendering for a large contract such as a hospital. Companies may need to submit several bids to try to ensure getting a contract.
The government has also promised legislation to remove a bureaucratic logjam which has prevented health service PFI projects from getting off the ground.
Health Minister Alan Milburn recently revealed that the previous government had spent 30 million pounds of Health Service funds on consultancy fees without securing a single PFI contract.
MORE EXPERIENCE NEEDED OF WORKING WITH PRIVATE SECTOR
The government must also ensure that its departments have more experience and understanding of working with the private sector.

One of the best known PFI contracts to date was the building of the Skye bridge, linking the Scottish island with the mainland over the strait where Bonnie Prince Charlie fled his English vanquishers in the 18th century.
The Scottish Office had estimated its part of the bill at six million pounds, but its outlays rose to 15 million by the time the bridge was opened in October 1995.

Design changes and delays contributed to the overrun, but the Scottish Office had also overlooked spending which should not have taken it by surprise -- such as two million pounds for advisers and another million for surveys, land purchase and staff, according to an inquiry by the National Audit Office.
When the 1-1/2 mile (1 km) long bridge opened, there were angry protests from Skye residents furious at the level of the tolls, which cost only a little less than the ferry it replaced.
The operator Miller/Dywidag was granted the right to charge tolls for 25 years to recoup its costs and is expected to make a hefty profit.

Yet another of the PFI's drawbacks was highlighted recently when the defence electronics company Racal Electronics pulled out of tendering for the 1.5 billion pound contract to develop an advanced radio communications system for police in England and Wales.
Racal said it dropped out, leaving British Telecom as the sole bidder, because there was no guarantee that the police would buy the system.
"We made a decision based on the commercial risks," said spokesman Nigel Edwards.
Despite its troubles, Labour and Britain's business community are convinced the PFI can still be a success with a few improvements, albeit drastic ones.

"The PFI, for all the teething problems, is beginning to deliver value and the new government's philosophy of public/private partnerships could lead to an extension of the PFI's role -- if we get the details right," said the CBI's Turner. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
